Three desks in Taylorsville share the work. The Property Valuation Administration (PVA) sets each parcel's value, the sheriff bills and takes payment, and the clerk's office picks up what is left after April 15. The sheriff never sets a value.

  • PVA, (502) 477-3207: assessments, exemption forms and questions about why a number changed.
  • Sheriff, (502) 477-3200: mails bills on October 1 and collects for the state, county and school districts, plus some cities and special districts such as fire protection and libraries when contracted to.
  • County attorney, (502) 477-3225: handles overdue bills from 7 West Main Street and sits with the PVA when an appeal reaches the local board.
  • County clerk, 2 West Main Street: keeps the certificates of delinquency and takes payment on any that remain unsold.

If the bill looks wrong, call the PVA first, and the sooner the better.

Bring your parcel number or the address when you call or visit, and write down who you spoke with. Each office holds a different piece of the file, so a seller usually needs a short conversation with the sheriff, the PVA and the clerk before listing.

Spencer County sits in the Louisville metro area, borders Jefferson County to the northwest, and has Taylorsville as its seat. Taylorsville Lake, mostly inside the county line, is a leading local draw. The county has grown fast: 11,766 people in 2000, 17,061 in 2010, 19,490 in 2020 and 20,998 estimated for July 2025.

It is a commuter county. The average trip to work is 32.7 minutes, and most buyers earn their pay elsewhere in the metro area. Because nearly nine in ten homes are owner occupied, most sales here are one family selling to another.

Owning here costs more than in much of Kentucky. Typical monthly outlay is $1,795 for owners carrying a mortgage and $532 for those who own free and clear. Households average 2.75 people, and 91.6 percent stayed in the same home during the last year. Only 4.1 percent of the 7,430 housing units tallied in 2020 sat empty, so homes tend to sell to buyers who plan to stay.

Seniors make up 18.1 percent of residents, a group that can use the homestead break covered below. Ask the sheriff for the exact bill on your parcel instead of estimating from the county median.

Bills carry a December 31 due date and go in the mail on October 1. The cost of timing is set by the collection statute:

  • Through November 1, pay 2 percent under the printed amount.
  • November 2 to December 31 is the printed amount, no more and no less.
  • January adds a 5 percent surcharge.
  • From February 1, the surcharge climbs to 10 percent and the sheriff's add-on fee joins it. The February to April 15 stretch carries a 21 percent penalty overall.

Escrow does not remove the need to look. The bill explains what to do when a mortgage company pays, and the sheriff's online lookup will show whether the lender actually sent the money before January begins.

Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency, and KRS 134.122 puts a lien on the real estate. The bill is also the personal obligation of the January 1 owner, with interest at 12 percent a year. Ninety days later, outside investors may buy it. The first offering is usually held in August or September.

Two things stop a sale: a payment agreement with the county attorney, or a foreclosure or bankruptcy case in which the county attorney is a party. The office also tries to reach the owner by regular mail ahead of any sale.

  • Still with the county: pay the full balance and accrued interest at the clerk's office, 2 West Main Street.
  • Already purchased: deal with the investor, who may tack on substantial administrative costs.
  • Payment plans: usually 4 to 8 months, and they must end before the next bill is due. Apply by the online form, by phone, or at 7 West Main Street, where an appointment shortens the wait. Sold certificates are not eligible.

Book a conference with the PVA first, because the process cannot begin anywhere else. After that meeting, the written appeal is filed at the clerk's office during the May window for viewing the roll, with a one-workday grace period at the end. A board of local owners then hears it about a month later.

The board wants paper: closed sales near you, an appraisal, a contractor's repair quote, an insurance declaration. If you bring none, it denies the appeal. A bill printed early uses your claimed figure, and a supplemental bill follows if the board lands higher. Ask the PVA which home sales it used for yours. That list is the fastest way to test the comparison, and parcels are physically reviewed at least every fourth year.

Owners past their 65th birthday, along with owners on a total-disability classification, can knock a fixed amount off the assessed value of the house they live in. The Department of Revenue put that amount at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. File Form 62A350 with the Spencer County PVA by December 31. An approved application carries forward while the applicant stays in the home, and a buyer must file a fresh one.

Under KRS 134.015, a delinquent bill is the January 1 owner's own debt, and its lien can outlast a change of ownership for up to eleven years. Buyers and title companies look for zero balances. Ask the sheriff for this year's payoff, then ask the clerk if any certificate exists and whether an investor bought it.

When a payment agreement with the county attorney is active, say so up front so the closing agent can include the remaining balance.

A practical order of work helps. Get the sheriff's written payoff. Visit or call the clerk at 2 West Main Street about older years. Call the county attorney at (502) 477-3225 if a plan is in place. Then hand all three to whoever runs the closing. A cash buyer can take the house with the balance paid from proceeds, and you avoid the wait that comes with a buyer's lender.

faqs.q: Who takes payment on a Spencer County bill?
faqs.a: The sheriff's office does, at (502) 477-3200. Look up the current bill on the sheriff's website, under the Property Taxes tab.

faqs.q: What changes once the April 15 cutoff passes in Spencer County?
faqs.a: The clerk takes over, a lien is recorded, and interest begins at 12 percent a year. After 90 more days an investor may buy the certificate, so call the county attorney before that point.

faqs.q: Does the Spencer County attorney offer payment plans?
faqs.a: Yes, for certificates that have not been sold. Plans generally last 4 to 8 months and must finish before the next bill is due. Call (502) 477-3225.

faqs.q: How big is the Spencer County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: The deduction is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period. Owners file with the PVA before the calendar year ends.

faqs.q: Can I list a Spencer County house that has past-due tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is settled out of the sale, since the lien does not lift until it is paid. Line up written figures from the sheriff and clerk first.
